bibliography.abstract: This paper examines how Seoul’s urban landscape sustains postcolonial forgetting not through neglect but through deliberate design. Across infrastructures, symbolic demolitions, and heritage zones, the city curates a spatial order that displaces historical confrontation in favor of emotional resolution. Drawing on theories of affect and postcolonial memory, it identifies three interlocking strategies of forgetting-by-design: infrastructural silence, where colonial systems are absorbed and obscured; affective demolition, where erasure is staged as public catharsis; and aesthetic simulation, where curated tradition masks rupture. Through case studies in Seoul—the colonial waterworks, the 1995–96 demolition of the Government-General Building, and the remaking of Bukchon Hanok Village and Gwanghwamun Square—it reveals how colonial inheritances are converted into symbolic comfort. These curated ruins do not critically engage with colonial afterlives; instead, they offer spectacle without reckoning, producing nationalism through managed absence. The contribution is twofold: first, to foreground infrastructure as an active agent of erasure and critique the contradictory system governing colonial legacies; second, to propose a conceptual tool for memory governance that reads curated ruins as systems of emotional and spatial management. Ultimately, repair will require not more remembrance, but different remembrance—grounded in accountability, spatial disclosure, and sustained engagement with imperial afterlives.
bibliography.title: Curated ruins: emotional governance and the memory politics of forgetting-by-design in postcolonial Seoul

en.caveats: The study relies on qualitative, historical case studies of high-profile symbolic sites in a single capital city, which may limit its direct application to everyday or non-capital postcolonial urban environments.
en.what: This paper analyzes Seoul's postcolonial urban landscape through case studies of the colonial waterworks, the 1995–1996 demolition of the Government-General Building, and the redevelopments of Bukchon Hanok Village and Gwanghwamun Square. It identifies three distinct strategies of 'forgetting-by-design'—infrastructural silence, affective demolition, and aesthetic simulation—to show how the city's spatial planning converts colonial legacies into nationalistic spectacles and emotional comfort rather than critical historical engagement.
en.why: It introduces a new conceptual framework for memory governance that demonstrates how urban infrastructure and deliberate spatial design can actively manage public emotion and erase colonial history, shifting the focus of postcolonial urban studies from simple neglect to highly curated, intentional erasure.
